title: Settlements (built-up areas)
summary: Every city, town, suburb, village, hamlet and roadside strip in Maine, classified with the Degree of Urbanisation (the UN-endorsed method for delineating cities, towns and rural areas) adapted to building footprints: building density on a 100 m grid decides what is a settlement and where it ends; the buildings themselves draw the outline. Used at zooms 5-12, where the 925k footprints are too dense to draw.

inputs.name: src_overture.buildings
inputs.role: Building footprints (Overture Maps): counted on the grid, and their outlines drawn around.

inputs.name: src_census.cousub
inputs.role: Towns (county subdivisions): each settlement is named after a town (for cities, towns and suburbs the one holding most of it).

inputs.name: src_census.county
inputs.role: County name, joined through the town GEOID.

inputs.name: app.settlement_edits
inputs.role: Manual edits drawn in the settlement editor, applied last.

steps.title: Why the Degree of Urbanisation
steps.detail: The Degree of Urbanisation (DEGURBA) was endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission in 2020 to delineate cities, towns and rural areas the same way everywhere. It classifies a grid by population density and then groups contiguous dense cells. Maine has no population grid fine enough for villages (the official grid is 1 km and needs 300+ people per km²), so buildings stand in for people: footprints are complete, current and 30 cm-accurate. v3 clustered buildings one by one, so a town's outline kept following houses along every road out of town (32 of 45 cities were long, thin shapes); a density grid stops where the density drops.

steps.title: Count buildings on a 100 m grid
steps.detail: Each footprint is projected to UTM 19N (EPSG:26919) and counted in the 100 m cell (1 hectare) holding a point on its surface. Its area is added to the cell's footprint cover.

steps.title: Density over 300 m
steps.detail: Each cell's density is measured over its 3×3 neighbourhood (9 ha), so one house or one empty lot does not decide a cell: buildings per hectare, and the share of ground covered by buildings. Cover lets a downtown or mill district of a few large buildings count as dense. DEGURBA uses population per km² on 1 km cells; 300 m windows suit Maine's small towns.

steps.title: Classify cells
steps.detail: Dense (the analogue of DEGURBA's urban-centre cells), semi-dense (its urban-cluster cells), low density and very low density. Statewide: 15,179 dense cells, 42,295 semi-dense, 132,009 low density; the rest of the cells with buildings are very low density. The grid is published as its own layer (Building density grid, hidden by default).
steps.math: \text{cell} = \begin{cases} \text{Dense} & d \ge 6 \ \lor\ c \ge 15\% \\ \text{Semi-dense} & d \ge 2.5 \ \lor\ c \ge 6\% \\ \text{Low density} & d \ge 1 \\ \text{Very low density} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

steps.title: Group contiguous cells into settlements
steps.detail: Dense and semi-dense cells connect to their 8 neighbours, and across a one-cell gap (a river, a highway, a park), as DEGURBA fills gaps. A group of 50 or more buildings is a settlement, classed by its size and how much of it is dense. A suburb is a weak-core settlement near a city; the same weak core far from a city is a rural service town (Ellsworth, Dover-Foxcroft, Fort Kent), so it stays a Town.
steps.math: \text{class} = \begin{cases} \text{City} & n \ge 2500 \\ \text{Suburb} & 500 \le n < 2500,\ \text{core} < 25\%,\ \le 15\ \text{km from a City} \\ \text{Town} & 500 \le n < 2500 \ \text{otherwise} \\ \text{Village} & 50 \le n < 500 \end{cases} \qquad \text{core} = \frac{n_{\text{dense cells}}}{n}

steps.title: Draw the outline from the buildings
steps.detail: A settlement's own footprints (those in its cells) are closed into one shape: buffered out 45 m to bridge the gaps between buildings, then back in 35 m, so the edge sits about 10 m beyond the outermost walls rather than on grid squares. Low-density ribbons along roads are not in the settlement's cells, so they no longer stretch its outline.

steps.title: Hamlets and roadside strips
steps.detail: Buildings outside every settlement are clustered wall to wall as in v3 (a building joins when at least 4 others are within 45 m), keeping groups of 10 or more, cut away where they overlap a settlement. Long, thin groups are roadside strips (houses lined along a road, DEGURBA's low-density rural ribbons); compact ones are hamlets, or villages from 50 buildings. Scattered houses are in no settlement.

steps.title: Fill holes, simplify, name
steps.detail: Holes smaller than 10 acres or 3 % of the settlement (parking lots, school fields) are filled; bigger ones (parks, ponds, rivers) stay. Simplified to 5 m. Named after the town containing a point on the settlement; a city, town or suburb spanning two towns is named after the one holding most of it (Lewiston-Auburn is Lewiston).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.detail: Portland: 24,095 buildings, 74 % of them in dense cells, so a City; it takes in Westbrook and the Portland peninsula but not South Portland (10,963 buildings, its own City across the Fore River). Ellsworth: 1,326 buildings on 650 acres with only 20 % in dense cells, the profile of a suburb, but no city is within 15 km, so it is a Town: the service centre of Hancock County. The rest of Ellsworth's built-up land is 24 hamlets and a roadside strip, kept apart from the town instead of stretching its outline along the roads.

steps.title: Manual edits
steps.detail: Polygons drawn by hand in the settlement editor are applied last, on top of the computed outlines, so they survive rebuilds and method changes. Remove: computed settlements are cut away inside the polygon. Replace: cut away likewise, then the drawn outline, exactly as drawn, becomes the settlement. Add: the drawn outline and every computed settlement it overlaps become one settlement. A partly cut settlement keeps its remaining parts of 1 acre or more and its class. Edited settlements get their buildings and footprint recounted, and may carry a name (instead of their town's) and a class (instead of the computed one, or for a drawn settlement the class from its building count). Applying takes seconds, so the map updates as soon as an edit is saved.

parameters.name: Grid cell
parameters.why: Fine enough for a village of a few streets; DEGURBA's 1 km cells would merge a Maine village into its surroundings or miss it.

parameters.name: Density window
parameters.why: Smooths single houses and empty lots; about the size of a village centre.

parameters.name: Dense cell
parameters.why: About the top 3.5 % of cells: downtown and older in-town neighbourhoods on small lots (roughly 1/4-acre lots with outbuildings), or commercial blocks of large buildings.

parameters.name: Semi-dense cell
parameters.why: With the dense cells, about the top 13 % of cells: suburban subdivisions and village streets (roughly 1-acre lots); below it is rural roadside and farm country.

parameters.name: Low-density cell
parameters.why: Rural residential; shown on the grid layer, not a settlement on its own.

parameters.name: Cell connectivity
parameters.why: Bridges a river, highway or park one cell wide, as DEGURBA's gap filling does, without chaining towns across open country.

parameters.name: Minimum settlement
parameters.why: Smaller dense groups are hamlets, drawn from the wall-to-wall clusters instead.

parameters.name: City / Town
parameters.why: Gives Maine's 19 urban areas as cities (Portland, Lewiston-Auburn, Biddeford-Saco, Bangor ...) and its service towns as towns.

parameters.name: Suburb
parameters.value: core < 25 % dense, within 15 km of a city
parameters.why: Separates commuter towns (Yarmouth, Windham, Kennebunk) from rural service towns with small cores.

parameters.name: Outline buffer out / in
parameters.why: As in v3: closes gaps between neighbouring buildings and leaves an edge about 10 m beyond the outermost walls.

parameters.name: Hamlet clustering
parameters.value: 45 m wall to wall, 4 neighbours, 10+ buildings
parameters.why: v3's method, now used only outside settlements.

parameters.name: Roadside strip
parameters.why: Oriented-rectangle elongation catches straight ribbons; Polsby-Popper catches winding ones.

parameters.name: Hole-filling threshold
parameters.why: Fills parking lots and school fields; keeps large parks, ponds and rivers.

parameters.name: Simplify tolerance
parameters.why: Smaller tiles without visibly changing outlines at zooms 5-12.

parameters.name: Edited remainder
parameters.why: What is left of a computed settlement after a remove or replace cuts through it stays a settlement if it is at least an acre; smaller slivers along the drawn edge are dropped.

parameters.name: Drawn outlines
parameters.why: The person drawing knows where the settlement ends; the outline is not snapped to the buildings or widened by the method's margin.

caveats: Buildings stand in for people: a block of seasonal camps counts like a year-round neighbourhood, and an apartment building counts as one building. Thresholds are calibrated to Maine and are not comparable with official DEGURBA population classes.
Scattered rural houses are in no settlement by design, so the buildings in settlements are well below the footprint count (about 341,000 of 925,000).
A lone large building far from others (a mill, warehouse or farm complex) is in no settlement unless its cover makes its cell dense or semi-dense.
Outlines follow buildings, so a settlement can have several parts where its cells connect across a gap the buildings do not bridge.

Rebuilt only when the number of building footprints or the method version (in the SQL) changes, about seven minutes. An Overture update that keeps the same count is not picked up; to force a rebuild run TRUNCATE src_units.settlements_meta, then ./mapgen apply maine-places.

Method history: v1 clustered one point per building (58 m); v2-v3 clustered footprints wall to wall (45 m), attaching large buildings and filling holes, which let towns stretch along roads. v4 (2026-10-05) classifies a density grid (Degree of Urbanisation) and keeps v3's clustering for hamlets.
Manual edits are judgement calls recorded with a note; the map shows edited outlines with a darker, heavier line (the source column says computed or edited).

references.title: Eurostat et al. (2021), Applying the Degree of Urbanisation: a methodological manual to define cities, towns and rural areas for international comparisons
references.note: the method this adapts (grid classes, contiguity, gap filling)

references.title: UN Statistical Commission (2020), A recommendation on the method to delineate cities, urban and rural areas for international statistical comparisons
references.note: endorsement of the Degree of Urbanisation for international comparisons (51st session, 2020)
